text.p: Many mutual fund investors trying to choose among the thousands of mutual funds available start by comparing performance records.
After all, if a fund has delivered solid returns over the past, say, five years, than it probably can continue to do well in the future.
Or can it?
Many investors discover that an outstanding long-term record doesn't always translate into superior returns in the future. That can happen for any number of reasons.
For example, the manager who generated those returns may leave the fund, turning over the reins to a less-experienced or less talented replacement.

The fund's investment style may fall from favour, causing the fund to slip into a prolonged slump. The manager may simply run out of luck, with a series of bad picks that create unpleasant surprises for shareholders. He may change his investment strategy, or make a large bet that doesn't pay off.
It's like they always say in the advertisements: Past performance is no guarantee of future results.
That said, past performance can help you choose mutual funds for your portfolio. But you must use the information properly, taking into account the factors that shape that performance.

When you are judging a fund's past returns, keep these points in mind: How did similar funds perform? It's not fair to compare the performance of an aggressive growth fund to the gains recorded by a bond fund, right?

Likewise, you wouldn't compare the record of a growth-and-income fund that aims for capital growth and current income to that of a growth fund that primarily pursues long-term growth. Each category of funds pursues different goals, and that results in different performances over short and long periods.

Thus, if you are looking for a growth-and-income fund, compare its returns to those of other growth-and-income funds. You can find out the average one-, three-, five- and 10-year returns of a fund category in Morningstar Mutual Funds, available at many libraries. Then compare those figures to the performance of the fund you are considering as an investment.

For example, balanced funds delivered 10.5 percent annual returns during the past three years, and 11 percent annually during the past five years. That compares with 10.3 percent and 14.3 percent, respectively, for the Lindner Dividend Fund (314-727-5305; $2,000 minimum investment; recent yield: 6.3 percent).

Sounds interesting -- but don't buy yet. Does the record reflect a consistent philosophy? Some funds generate solid returns by chasing fads -- they buy whatever is hot this year, and then switch to the next hot sector next year. When that strategy works, it can deliver strong gains. But what if your manager jumps to the wrong trend, or the current hot sector collapses before he gets out?
Ideally, you should invest in funds that choose a consistent investment approach.

For example, Morningstar notes that Lindner Dividend Fund manager Eric Ryback buys securities that meet strict value criteria and pay above-average dividends, focusing on individual security selection rather than trendy sector plays.

A quick search using the library's computer or your own will turn up several magazine articles confirming that Ryback has maintained a consistent investment philosophy through a variety of market conditions.
What risks did the fund incur? A call to the fund company will turn up information about how it has performed in different market conditions.

You can bolster that information by reading magazine and other articles about the fund, and by checking the fund profile in Morningstar or in the Value Line Survey of Mutual Funds. In this case, it turns out that the Lindner Dividend Fund has been 41 percent less volatile than the average balanced fund during the past three years, and 64 percent less volatile during the past five years.

The upshot: Lindner Dividend not only has a strong performance record in its category and is driven by a consistent investment philosophy, it also has kept risk well in hand. Those factors are still no guarantee that the fund will do well in the future -- but they are about as close as you're going to get to such assurance.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
